title: Love of the law as wisdom, endurance, and imitation of God
english: The unjust are blind to the beauty of righteousness and do not see clearly the dignity and grace of the words about it. But the one who has chosen these words and wished to belong to them—this person alone is established in understanding, because wisdom reveals her own beauty only to her lovers, as it is written: “Love her, and she will honor you; honor her, that she may embrace you” (Proverbs 4:6, 8).

All good things in a person come through practice, and so he was extended along with the intensity of his practice, so that through it he surpassed the elder, the young man, and the disciple—surpassing his teachers.
Presenting himself as humble and obedient, he asks for the salvation that comes from this, from God who gives grace to the humble and has promised mercy to those who love him (Ps 118:107).

It is a greater proof of eagerness to pass through dangers and not stand away from the law, and to be in the midst of plots and not be dragged away from righteous things by anger and irritation toward those plotting against him (Ps 118:109-110). Thus Saul’s plot did not lead David astray into avenging himself, even where that might have seemed fitting.

He intensified the demonstration of his zeal for the law when he said he had set the law as his own inheritance, choosing to live in it not for a time but forever, not as under a yoke of necessity but holily in gladness of soul. For what is done with gladness is lasting and hard to overturn.

Even if they are not hateful insofar as they are human, it is not unworthy of God that such people are said to be hateful to God, according to the words: “You hated all who work lawlessness” (Psalm 5:6 (5:5)) (Ps 118:113). So the greatest proof of loving the law is hating those who have turned aside from the law. For this reason Jehoshaphat’s friendship with such a person became a reproach through the prophet, because he loved the one hated by God (Ps 118:118-119).

He shows an imitation of God. If every apostate from the ordinances is made worthless by God for his vain thoughts, then to him also they appear no more valuable than grape-pressings or dross. Therefore he is stirred up to love of the divine commands, taking the vanity of the wicked as an encouragement to care for what is good. The fifth edition reads: “They were counted as nothing.”

He longs for what is lacking to be filled up by God’s forbearance, since God waits for the good work that is still to come, as if guaranteeing that it will be fulfilled—just as those who guarantee debtors do so to keep them from falling badly into deceptions (Ps 118:122). Symmachus says: “Receive me, your servant, for good,” and Aquila and Theodotion rendered: “Be my guarantee” (Ps 118:122).
Others, he says, admire gold and precious stones, but I, knowing the divine commandments to be the only wonderful and beautiful thing, hold to them and guard them more than any treasure (Ps 118:130).

The oracles need to be opened. Therefore the Lord opened the mind of the disciples to understand the Scriptures (Luke 24:45), and the understanding given through the words drives away the deception that comes through pleasure or glory (Ps 118:130).
He asks for this because precision about sound teaching is difficult amid disturbances and griefs (Ps 118:134).
See the enmity that the righteous have (Ps 118:139). This was enmity toward their injustice and their forgetfulness of the law.

According to the history, the words can be referred to David speaking about himself. For he was the youngest of all the sons of Jesse, and also despised. When all his brothers were taken by their father to the feast that Samuel had prepared, David was with his father’s sheep and was not taken to the banquet. Yet although he was younger and despised, he himself received the kingdom by God’s decision, since he had not forgotten the ordinances of God. The one who is being instructed in the divine words is also younger and despised because he humbles himself. And the people called from the nations after the elder and firstborn Israel could also speak this verse.

orientation: Apollinaris is commenting on verses of Psalm 118 (119), explaining how the psalmist's love for God's law brings understanding, endurance under persecution, and imitation of God's own judgments.
